name: Titanium dioxide
lead: Titanium dioxide (TiO2), also called titanium white or CI 77891, is a white, water-insoluble mineral compound and the most widely used white pigment. It is found in paints, plastics, paper and toothpaste as well as cosmetics [1]. In skincare it serves as a mineral (physical) UV filter and as a pigment in tinted products.

In sunscreen it is usually paired with zinc oxide. Wikipedia describes mineral filters as working mainly by absorbing UV, with some reflection and scattering, and notes that titanium dioxide gives good protection but does not fully cover the UVA range; zinc oxide has been reported to be superior at 340 to 380 nm [2]. Since 2019 the FDA has sorted UV filters into categories, and as of 2021 only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were recognised as generally recognised as safe and effective (GRASE) [2].

Safety discussion centres on nanoparticle forms and on inhalation. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies inhaled titanium dioxide dust as Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans, and advises against sprayable sunscreens because of inhalation risk [1]. The EU withdrew authorisation of E171 as a food additive in 2022 after the European Food Safety Authority could not rule out genotoxicity; this does not concern its use in sunscreen [1][3].

paras: Titanium dioxide is used in sunscreens, foundations, powders and tinted SPF, typically as a pigment at low single-digit percentages in colour cosmetics [3]. Nano-sized particles give a sheerer finish, and cited studies report higher SPF than equal concentrations of larger particles [3]. Mineral sunscreens made with larger particles can leave an opaque white cast that consumers often reject, and people may apply them less thickly, which reduces effective protection [2]. Adding iron oxide or pigmentary titanium dioxide has been reported to improve visible-light protection [2].

Beyond skincare, it is used as a food whitener (E171), in toothpaste and in paints, which consume roughly half of world production [1][3]. Its photocatalytic properties, discovered by Akira Fujishima, underpin self-cleaning and anti-fogging coatings and solar-cell research [1][4][5].

The compound scatters and reflects light and absorbs UV. Anatase is more photoactive than rutile: under UV light it generates hydroxyl radicals [3]. Coatings of alumina or silica are used on cosmetic and paint grades to improve dispersion and weather resistance [3].

Non-nano particles stay largely in the outer skin layer, and Grokipedia, citing studies, reports about 5% reaching the upper epidermis and about 0.1% the dermis with no significant systemic absorption after repeated use; that page itself contains uncited statements [3]. A 2012 study examined titanium dioxide nanoparticles in food and personal care products as sources of environmental release [6]. A 2015 study found titanium dioxide nanoparticles under UV light increased hydrogen peroxide, which can damage phytoplankton, and environmental advocates often recommend mineral sunscreens for reef protection as a precaution [2]. About 99% of nanoparticles reaching wastewater end up in sewage sludge [1].

IARC (2010) classified titanium dioxide Group 2B largely on high-dose rat inhalation data; Grokipedia argues human worker cohorts show no consistent excess of lung cancer [3]. In 2025 the Court of Justice of the EU upheld the annulment of the CLP classification of certain titanium dioxide powders as an inhalation carcinogen, with the food ban unaffected [3].

A registered phase 4 study (NCT01021787, started 2009, n=26) examined dermal penetration of titanium dioxide from an SPF40 sunscreen cream in volunteers [7]. No published results were identified in the available sources. Other registered trials involving titanium dioxide are dental or environmental and unrelated to skin appearance.

Mineral sunscreens and tinted SPF containing titanium dioxide are discussed in skincare communities as options for sensitive skin or for preferring non-chemical filters, set against concerns over white cast. These are general sunscreen discussions rather than claims specific to the compound.

card.summary: The classic mineral UV filter and white pigment in physical sunscreens and tinted SPF; broad but weaker on UVA I.
card.note: Inhalation concerns (IARC 2B) apply to dust and sprays; EU banned E171 in food, not in sunscreen.

quick.overview:
Titanium dioxide is a white mineral used as a physical sunscreen filter and a pigment in tinted SPF. Together with zinc oxide it was the only filter the FDA recognised as GRASE as of 2021.

It gives good UVB and UVA II coverage but is weaker in UVA I, and larger particles can leave a white cast.
quick.mechanism: It scatters and reflects light and absorbs UV. Nano-sized particles give a sheerer finish.
quick.risks: IARC classes inhaled dust as Group 2B and advises against sprayable sunscreens. The EU removed it as a food additive in 2022. Non-nano particles mostly stay in the outer skin layer, though nanoparticle effects on aquatic life are studied.
